paras: The Orange, Texas, lynchings of 1881 were the killings of several Black men by armed white citizens of Orange, Texas, on August 17-21, 1881, after Sheriff George W. Michael was shot pursuing Sam Saxon and others. Robert Saxon was hanged from an oak in town, others were shot, and on August 21 an armed party took Sam Saxon and another prisoner from the jail and shot them. Reported deaths ranged from three to eight, and the killings drew national wire coverage and a protest by Black residents of Galveston.

A Houston dispatch traced the violence to a feud: after a detective shot O. L. Delano, his brother Charles, a white man, blamed the sheriff and plotted with Dug Harris and Sam and Bob Saxon to kill him. A Globe-Democrat correspondent described instead a six-year feud between townsmen and country families, with Delano's following including "some eight or ten negroes," among them the Saxons.

Shortly after dark on August 17, Sam Saxon and two or three other Black men were reported to have attacked a white man, Gus Garvey, in the Sample Room Saloon, where shots were fired but no one was hurt. Sheriff Michael, Deputy Ferguson and a few others followed, and near "negro town" the posse was fired on, a shotgun charge striking the sheriff in the right arm and side. The Orange Tribune said the Black men had been "lying in ambush"; the posse fired back and shot down Sam Saxon and another man.

Believing the sheriff mortally wounded, about 150 armed citizens took up the pursuit. By morning Robert Saxon, Sam's brother, hung from the large oak in front of D. Call & Son's store, and two others were dead. Houston dispatches said citizens shot four captured Black men and hanged Bob Saxon after extorting a confession. Charles Delano and several Black men were jailed under guard of the Orange Rifles.

Sam Saxon, wounded and pursued, gave himself up on Sunday morning, August 21. That evening the Rifles left the jail, and about 9 o'clock an armed party surrounded it; Deputy Sheriff Rance Jett, facing an overpowering force, gave it up. The party took out Saxon and an unnamed Black prisoner and, as both cried "murder," filled them with buckshot at a spot the papers do not name, while church congregations scattered.

Charles Delano, threatened with trial by "Judge Lynch," was instead bailed, at $2,000 per the San Marcos Free Press, and left the county. The rest of the "lawless gang" were ordered out of the county, and no report of an inquest or of charges against the killers appears. On August 24, 300 Black residents of Galveston met to denounce the "bloody outrages perpetrated on negroes" and Governor Roberts's refusal to interfere.

The first Galveston News wire, blaming Black men "instigated by some white men," ran in the Savannah Morning News, the New York Sun and the Rock Island Argus. From August 23 a longer Houston dispatch ran nationally under headlines such as "Lynch Law in Texas."

Papers near Orange took the townsmen's view: the Orange Tribune called the hanging "a natural result of the rage and indignation of the community," and a Houston dispatch called it "the comparatively sober act of an organized band of citizens."

Criticism came from the Lake Charles Commercial, which described a "reign of terror" no official tried to stop, and from the Globe-Democrat, whose correspondent wrote that the prisoners were "shot down like dogs." The Houston Post, quoted by the San Marcos Free Press, said excitement "cannot justify the violence" but kept its sharpest words for Delano's release. Midwestern papers carried a brief on the Galveston resolutions condemning the "butchery of innocent negroes by the mob at Orange."

Death tolls ran from three in the first wire to seven in the New Orleans Times and eight in the Evening Critic. The New Orleans Times named Bob rather than Sam Saxon as the man taken from jail, and the Evening Critic alone said the Delanos were killed, which the reports of Charles Delano's bail contradict. The ambush account came from the sheriff's side, and the Globe-Democrat correspondent wrote that it had not been established that the Saxon party fired first.

reader.title: Orange, Texas, lynchings of 1881
bases: After a sheriff's posse was fired on, armed citizens hanged Robert Saxon and shot several Black men without trial (A31, A7), and a crowd took Sam Saxon and another Black prisoner from the county jail and shot them (A32, A26).

The local Orange Tribune (A31), the Galveston News correspondent (A32), the New Orleans Democrat (A26) and Houston and Galveston wires (A4, A7) independently report the posse fight, the hanging and the jail killing, though they disagree on the toll.

accounts.label: Galveston News wire (first report)
accounts.gist: Sheriff 'Mitchell' wounded by Black men 'instigated by some white men'; the posse killed three, one of them hanged; military and citizens keeping order.

accounts.label: Orange Tribune (local, townsmen's version)
accounts.gist: Black men lay in ambush and fired on the posse; 150 citizens pursued them, and by morning Robert Saxon hung from an oak, two others were dead and Delano was jailed as an originator of a plot to kill the sheriff.

accounts.label: St. Louis Republican wire from Houston
accounts.gist: The violence grew from Delano's feud with the sheriff; citizens shot four Black men, hanged Bob Saxon after extorting a confession, hanged another, and later took Sam Saxon and another from the jail and shot them.

accounts.label: Evening Critic Houston dispatch
accounts.gist: A committee of 150 voted to lynch the gang; eight were lynched, including Robert hanged six times, Sam Saxon and Charles Delano shot escaping, and O. L. Delano hanged to a telegraph pole.

accounts.label: Galveston News correspondent and New Orleans Democrat (jail killing)
accounts.gist: Sam Saxon surrendered Sunday morning; that night an armed party took the jail from Deputy Jett and shot Saxon and another prisoner after they begged for mercy.

accounts.label: Globe-Democrat correspondent
accounts.gist: A six-year feud underlay the violence; it was not established that the Saxon party fired first or lay in ambush; the jail prisoners were shot clinging to the officers' knees.

framing.detail: The Orange Tribune, reprinted in the Lake Charles Echo, called the killing and hanging 'a natural result of the rage and indignation of the community'.
The New Orleans Times telegram headed 'Citizens Determined to Wipe out the Lawless Element' and called the dead 'negro roughs' and 'desperadoes'.
The Evening Critic's dispatch called it 'the comparatively sober act of an organized band of citizens'.
National papers ran the Houston wire under 'Lynch Law in Texas', 'A Reign of Terror' and 'Ambushes, Murders and Lynchings'.
The Lake Charles Commercial called it a 'reign of terror' that officials made no attempt to stop.
The Globe-Democrat dispatch said the prisoners were 'shot down like dogs' by a mob and doubted the ambush story.

The Houston Post, quoted by the San Marcos Free Press, said the excitement could not justify the violence but reserved its strongest words for Delano's release; the Free Press faulted Orange for not lynching or trying him.

conflicts.note: Early counts predate the August 21 jail killing; the Commercial called all reports 'meagre and unreliable'.
